claims.text: High-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings have superior resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation compared with monolithic HEA coatings.
The superior creep resistance of the multilayer coatings is caused by their nanoscale multilayer interfaces.
Nanoscale multilayer interfaces impede dislocation motion and thereby reduce creep strain relative to monolithic HEA coatings.
The as-deposited coatings consist of alternating layers having distinct grain sizes, crystallographies, or phase structures.
Reducing constituent-layer thickness increases interface density in the multilayer coatings.
Testing at 600–800°C under constant sub-yield stress ensures deformation in the creep regime.
Creep behavior in HEAs is sensitive to applied stress and temperature.
Nanoscale multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation nucleation, glide, and cross-slip.
Multilayer interfaces produce a more uniform distribution of strain.
Time-dependent deformation in the proposed coatings is governed by dislocation activity.
Interfaces interrupt dislocation paths and promote interfacial strain redistribution.
Interfacial strain redistribution limits localized plastic-strain accumulation and retards creep.
Thinner layers and higher interface density will produce a lower steady-state creep strain rate than a monolithic coating under identical conditions.
Thinner layers and higher interface density will reduce total creep deformation relative to a monolithic coating.
Monolithic HEA coatings have higher creep rates because they lack engineered interfaces and permit relatively uninhibited dislocation motion.
The proposed interface-mediated effect applies at layer thicknesses of approximately 10–100 nm.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure may cause interdiffusion that blurs the multilayer interfaces and alters the effect.
